meta.title: Theorem Atlas
meta.subtitle: The dependency graph of AP Calculus AB — every concept, what it leans on, and where you stand.
meta.scope: AP Calculus AB only. No series, no parametric/polar/vector, no integration by parts, no improper integrals (all BC topics). Alpha: the map is the product.

nodes.title: Limit of a function (intuitive)
nodes.statement: We write \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) to mean: as \(x\) gets arbitrarily close to \(a\) (from either side), \(f(x)\) gets arbitrarily close to \(L\). The value \(f(a)\) itself is irrelevant — it may not even exist.
nodes.notes: Everything in calculus is a limit in disguise: derivatives, integrals, even continuity. If this node is shaky, the whole map wobbles.

nodes.title: Epsilon–delta definition of limit
nodes.statement: \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) means: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - a| < \delta\) implies \(|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\).
nodes.notes: Not tested on the AP exam, but this is the bridge to real analysis: it turns 'arbitrarily close' into something you can prove things with. Enrichment, not required.

nodes.title: Limit laws
nodes.statement: If \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x)\) and \(\lim_{x\to a} g(x)\) exist, then limits respect sums, differences, products, quotients (denominator nonzero), powers, and roots: e.g. \(\lim (f+g) = \lim f + \lim g\).
nodes.proof_sketch: The sum law from epsilon–delta: given \(\varepsilon\), pick \(\delta_1\) making \(|f - L| < \varepsilon/2\) and \(\delta_2\) making \(|g - M| < \varepsilon/2\); take \(\delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2)\) and apply the triangle inequality.
nodes.notes: The workhorse you use without thinking. Every derivative rule proof leans on these.

nodes.title: Squeeze theorem
nodes.statement: If \(g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)\) near \(a\) and \(\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = \lim_{x\to a} h(x) = L\), then \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L\).
nodes.proof_sketch: From \(|g - L| < \varepsilon\) and \(|h - L| < \varepsilon\) we get \(L - \varepsilon < g \le f \le h < L + \varepsilon\), so \(|f - L| < \varepsilon\).
nodes.notes: How you prove limits you can't compute directly — most famously the \(\sin h / h\) lemma.

nodes.title: The \(\sin h / h\) lemma
nodes.statement: \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h} = 1\).
nodes.proof_sketch: For small \(h > 0\), geometry gives \(\sin h < h < \tan h\). Divide by \(\sin h\): \(1 < h/\sin h < 1/\cos h\). Take reciprocals and squeeze as \(h \to 0^+\); evenness handles \(h < 0\).
nodes.notes: The single fact that unlocks all trig derivatives. Worth memorizing the picture, not just the result.

nodes.title: Limits at infinity & infinite limits
nodes.statement: \(\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L\) describes end behavior (horizontal asymptotes); \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = \infty\) describes blow-up (vertical asymptotes). Computed with limit laws plus dominance: highest power wins.
nodes.notes: The language of asymptotes and end behavior — you need it for curve sketching later.

nodes.title: Continuity at a point
nodes.statement: \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) if \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)\): the limit exists, the value exists, and they agree. Three ways to fail: hole, jump, blow-up.
nodes.notes: Continuity is the hypothesis of every big existence theorem on this map (IVT, EVT). Always check it first.

nodes.title: Intermediate Value Theorem
nodes.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(N\) is between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\), then some \(c\) in \((a,b)\) has \(f(c) = N\).
nodes.proof_sketch: Bisect: keep the half-interval whose endpoints straddle \(N\). Nested intervals shrink to a point \(c\); continuity forces \(f(c) = N\).
nodes.notes: Why you're allowed to say 'the equation has a solution' — the theoretical backbone of root-finding.

nodes.title: Extreme Value Theorem
nodes.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on a closed interval \([a,b]\), then \(f\) attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum there.
nodes.notes: Proof needs completeness of the reals — beyond AB scope. What matters: it guarantees max/min exist, so optimization isn't wishful thinking. Closed interval + continuity are both essential (know the counterexamples).

nodes.title: Derivative as a limit
nodes.statement: \(f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\), when the limit exists. Instantaneous rate of change; slope of the tangent line.
nodes.notes: The second master definition after limits. Almost every differentiation rule is proved by feeding it through this limit plus the limit laws.

nodes.title: Differentiability implies continuity
nodes.statement: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(a\). (The converse is false: \(|x|\) at 0.)
nodes.proof_sketch: Write \(f(x) - f(a) = \frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\cdot(x-a)\). Take \(x \to a\): the fraction tends to \(f'(a)\) and \((x-a) \to 0\), so \(f(x) \to f(a)\).
nodes.notes: A two-line proof that upgrades every differentiability hypothesis into a continuity hypothesis for free.

nodes.title: Power rule
nodes.statement: \(\frac{d}{dx}[x^n] = nx^{n-1}\) for (at least) positive integer \(n\); extends to all real \(n\).
nodes.proof_sketch: For integer \(n\): expand \((x+h)^n\) with the binomial theorem; every term but \(nx^{n-1}h\) has \(h^2\) or higher, so they vanish in the difference quotient limit.
nodes.notes: First rule you learn, and the template for how rules get proved: definition + limit laws + algebra.

nodes.title: Product rule
nodes.proof_sketch: The add-and-subtract trick: \(f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x) = [f(x+h)-f(x)]g(x+h) + f(x)[g(x+h)-g(x)]\). Divide by \(h\), take limits; continuity of \(g\) (from differentiability) handles \(g(x+h) \to g(x)\).
nodes.notes: Watch where continuity of \(g\) sneaks in — that's the differentiability-implies-continuity node doing quiet work.

nodes.title: Quotient rule
nodes.statement: \(\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}\) (where \(g \ne 0\)).
nodes.proof_sketch: Follows from the product rule applied to \(f \cdot g^{-1}\) plus the chain rule — or directly from the definition with the same add-subtract trick.
nodes.notes: Low over high minus high over low, over low-low. Memorize via the product-rule derivation, not the rhyme.

nodes.title: Chain rule
nodes.statement: \(\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\).
nodes.proof_sketch: Idea: \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u}\cdot\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}\). The subtlety: \(\Delta u\) can be zero, so a fully rigorous proof needs a patch (define the difference quotient to be \(f'(u_0)\) when \(\Delta u = 0\)). AB-level intuition via differentials is fine.
nodes.notes: The most-used rule in calculus. Also the engine behind implicit differentiation, related rates, and u-substitution.

nodes.title: Derivatives of sine and cosine
nodes.statement: \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\), \(\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x\).
nodes.proof_sketch: Apply the definition to \(\sin\): the difference quotient becomes \(\sin x\cdot\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x\cdot\frac{\sin h}{h}\). The \(\sin h/h \to 1\) lemma plus \((\cos h-1)/h \to 0\) (multiply by \((\cos h+1)/(\cos h+1)\)) finish it.
nodes.notes: This is why the \(\sin h/h\) lemma exists. One lemma, all of trigonometry's calculus.

nodes.title: Derivatives of \(e^x\) and \(\ln x\)
nodes.statement: \(\frac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x\); \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}\).
nodes.proof_sketch: For \(\ln\): differentiate \(e^{\ln x} = x\) implicitly — \(e^{\ln x}\cdot(\ln x)' = 1\), so \((\ln x)' = 1/x\). For \(e^x\): it's the inverse-function mirror of the same fact.
nodes.notes: \(e^x\) being its own derivative is the reason exponential models are everywhere. The \(\ln\) proof is a great first implicit-differentiation payoff.

nodes.title: Derivatives of inverse trig functions
nodes.statement: \(\frac{d}{dx}\arcsin x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\), \(\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}\) (and similarly for the rest).
nodes.proof_sketch: Let \(y = \arcsin x\), so \(\sin y = x\). Differentiate implicitly: \(\cos y \cdot y' = 1\), so \(y' = 1/\cos y = 1/\sqrt{1-x^2}\) (using \(\cos^2 y = 1 - \sin^2 y\)).
nodes.notes: Pure implicit differentiation in action — no new ideas, just the technique applied to inverse relationships.

nodes.title: Implicit differentiation
nodes.statement: To differentiate an equation \(F(x,y) = 0\): differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\) (chain rule), then solve for \(y'\).
nodes.notes: Not a theorem — a technique. It's the chain rule wearing a costume, and it powers related rates, inverse-function derivatives, and tons of AP free-response.

nodes.title: Related rates
nodes.statement: When quantities are linked by an equation and all vary with time, differentiate the equation with respect to \(t\) (chain rule / implicit differentiation) and solve for the unknown rate.
nodes.notes: A word-problem protocol more than a theorem: draw, label, write the relation, differentiate, substitute. The calculus is easy; the setup is the skill.

nodes.title: Fermat's theorem (interior extrema)
nodes.statement: If \(f\) has a local max or min at \(c\) and \(f'(c)\) exists, then \(f'(c) = 0\).
nodes.proof_sketch: At a local max, the difference quotient \([f(c+h)-f(c)]/h\) is \(\le 0\) for \(h > 0\) and \(\ge 0\) for \(h < 0\). The two-sided limit can only be 0.
nodes.notes: Why critical points matter at all. Note the hypothesis 'derivative exists' — corners and cusps are critical points too, via the definition.

nodes.title: Rolle's theorem
nodes.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a) = f(b)\), then some \(c\) in \((a,b)\) has \(f'(c) = 0\).
nodes.proof_sketch: By EVT, \(f\) attains a max and min on \([a,b]\). If both are at endpoints they're equal (constant function, derivative 0 everywhere); otherwise an interior extremum exists and Fermat gives \(f'(c) = 0\).
nodes.notes: The hinge of the whole applications chapter: MVT is one clever auxiliary function away.

nodes.title: Mean Value Theorem
nodes.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then some \(c\) in \((a,b)\) has \(f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\).
nodes.proof_sketch: Tilt the graph flat: apply Rolle's to \(g(x) = f(x) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\,x\), which satisfies \(g(a) = g(b)\).
nodes.notes: The most load-bearing theorem in first-year calculus: it justifies the first derivative test, L'Hôpital, error bounds, and half of analysis later.

nodes.title: First derivative test
nodes.statement: If \(f'\) changes from + to − at \(c\), \(f\) has a local max there; − to +, a local min. (Consequence of MVT: sign of \(f'\) controls increase/decrease.)
nodes.proof_sketch: MVT on \([a,c]\) and \([c,b]\): \(f'\) positive forces \(f\) up, negative forces it down. Sign change pins the extremum.
nodes.notes: The practical classification tool. Draw the sign chart — it's MVT made mechanical.

nodes.title: Second derivative test & concavity
nodes.statement: If \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) > 0\), local min at \(c\) (reverse for max). Concavity: \(f'' > 0\) means concave up; sign changes of \(f''\) locate inflection points.
nodes.proof_sketch: Second derivative test: \(f''(c) > 0\) means \(f'\) is increasing through 0 at \(c\) — so \(f'\) goes − to +, and the first derivative test applies.
nodes.notes: Inconclusive when \(f''(c) = 0\) — fall back to the first derivative test. That's a favorite AP trap.

nodes.title: Optimization
nodes.statement: To optimize: express the quantity as a function of one variable, find critical points (Fermat), and use EVT (closed interval) or the first derivative test to certify the extremum.
nodes.notes: Where EVT stops being abstract: it guarantees your critical-point hunt actually finds the global max. Always check endpoints on closed intervals.

nodes.title: L'Hôpital's rule
nodes.statement: If \(\lim f/g\) is \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\) (and hypotheses hold), then \(\lim_{x\to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}\).
nodes.proof_sketch: Follows from Cauchy's MVT: \([f(x)-f(a)]/[g(x)-g(a)] = f'(c)/g'(c)\) for \(c\) between \(a\) and \(x\). The full proof is beyond AB — know when it applies (indeterminate form, differentiability) instead.
nodes.notes: Check the hypotheses before you fire it: indeterminate form required. \(\lim_{x\to 0} \sin x / x\) doesn't need it — and using it there is circular, since the \(\sin h/h\) lemma came first.

nodes.title: Antiderivative
nodes.statement: \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) if \(F' = f\). Antiderivatives differ by a constant (MVT corollary): the indefinite integral \(\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C\).
nodes.notes: Differentiation run backwards. The '+ C' isn't decoration — it's the MVT consequence that functions with the same derivative differ by a constant.

nodes.title: Riemann sums
nodes.statement: Partition \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals; a Riemann sum \(\sum f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x\) approximates signed area. Left, right, midpoint, trapezoidal are choices of sample points \(x_i^*\).
nodes.notes: The integral's origin story: area as a limit of rectangles. Every 'set up the integral' problem starts here conceptually.

nodes.title: Definite integral
nodes.statement: \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x\): the limit of Riemann sums — net signed area under the curve.
nodes.notes: Two big ideas fused: a limit and an accumulation. Keep them separate in your head and FTC becomes obvious instead of miraculous.

nodes.title: Properties of definite integrals
nodes.statement: Linearity, additivity over intervals (\(\int_a^b = \int_a^c + \int_c^b\)), reversal (\(\int_a^b = -\int_b^a\)), and comparison (\(f \le g \Rightarrow \int f \le \int g\)).
nodes.proof_sketch: All inherited from the corresponding properties of finite sums, passed through the limit.
nodes.notes: The quiet toolkit behind every integral manipulation. Additivity over intervals is what makes piecewise and absolute-value integrals work.

nodes.title: Fundamental Theorem, Part 1
nodes.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt\) is differentiable and \(g'(x) = f(x)\): differentiation undoes accumulation.
nodes.proof_sketch: The difference quotient \([g(x+h)-g(x)]/h\) is the average value of \(f\) over \([x,x+h]\); as \(h \to 0\), continuity squeezes that average to \(f(x)\).
nodes.notes: Why every accumulation function has an elementary derivative. This is the half of FTC that justifies 'integral of a rate is net change'.

nodes.title: Fundamental Theorem, Part 2
nodes.statement: If \(F' = f\) on \([a,b]\), then \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)\): definite integrals evaluated by antiderivatives.
nodes.proof_sketch: Let \(G(x) = \int_a^x f\). By FTC1, \(G' = f = F'\), so \(G - F\) is constant (MVT); evaluating at \(a\) pins the constant, and \(x = b\) gives the formula.
nodes.notes: The evaluation half — the reason you spent weeks on antiderivatives. Notice the proof chains FTC1 + MVT: the map's two biggest threads meeting.

nodes.title: U-substitution
nodes.statement: \(\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du\) with \(u = g(x)\): the chain rule run backwards. For definite integrals, change the bounds (\(u = g(a)\), \(u = g(b)\)) instead of back-substituting.
nodes.notes: Pattern recognition skill: spot the inner function \(g\) and check its derivative is sitting nearby (up to a constant). Definite-integral bound-changing is the AP favorite.

nodes.title: Area between curves
nodes.statement: Area between \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = g(x)\) from \(a\) to \(b\): \(\int_a^b |f - g|\,dx\). Split at intersection points where the top function changes.
nodes.notes: An application, not a theorem — it's the definite integral plus geometry. Sketch first; the picture tells you the bounds and the top/bottom.

nodes.title: Volumes by disks & washers
nodes.statement: Revolve a region about an axis: cross-sections are disks (\(\pi r^2\)) or washers (\(\pi(R^2 - r^2)\)). Volume = \(\int \pi(\text{radius})^2\,dx\).
nodes.notes: Riemann sums in 3D: each thin slice is (approximately) a disk, and the integral is the limit. Same idea as area, one dimension up.

nodes.title: Average value of a function
nodes.statement: \(f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). (MVT for integrals: a continuous \(f\) attains this value at some \(c\).)
nodes.notes: The continuous analogue of averaging a list. Shows up in 'average rate' and motion problems.

nodes.title: Slope fields
nodes.statement: For \(dy/dx = F(x,y)\), a slope field draws the tangent slope at a grid of points; solution curves follow the slopes. A picture of a differential equation's solutions without solving it.
nodes.notes: Qualitative before quantitative: you can sketch solution behavior (growth, equilibria) straight from the field.

nodes.title: Separable differential equations
nodes.statement: If \(dy/dx = g(x)h(y)\), separate: \(\int \frac{dy}{h(y)} = \int g(x)\,dx\), integrate both sides (antiderivatives + u-sub), solve for \(y\), use the initial condition.
nodes.notes: AB's capstone technique: it chains antiderivatives, u-substitution, and algebra. Exponential growth/decay models live here.
